l_3e63550b842e.title: Ratio language and notation
l_3e63550b842e.summary: Students describe relationships with part-to-part and part-to-whole ratios, using the words 'to' and 'for every' and the notation 3:2.

segments.title: Describe the fruit bowl
segments.description:
Draw a bowl on the board with 3 apples and 2 bananas.
Ask students to write one sentence that compares the fruit using numbers.
Collect a few answers and write them on the board without correcting them yet.
segments.teacherNotes: Expect ‘there are more apples’, ‘5 fruits’ and ‘3 apples and 2 bananas’. Praise any statement that uses both numbers. Say that today they will learn a precise way to write comparisons. Use drawings only; no real food.

segments.title: Three ways to write a ratio
segments.description:
Using the same bowl, write ‘for every 3 apples there are 2 bananas’, then 3:2, then 3 to 2. Say that all three mean the same ratio of apples to bananas.
Show the apples to all fruit ratio as 3:5. Label the first ratio part-to-part and the second part-to-whole.
Switch the order to bananas to apples and write 2:3. Ask students why 2:3 is not the same ratio as 3:2.
Students copy a three-column note: words, a:b, a to b.
segments.teacherNotes: Common mistake: writing 3:2 for apples to all fruit because they forget the whole is 3 + 2 = 5. Also, a ratio is not a fraction here; avoid writing it as 3/2. Stress reading the order from the words: ‘apples to bananas’ puts apples first.

segments.title: Write it and name it
segments.description:
Show five situations one at a time on the board. For each, students write the ratio as a:b on a mini whiteboard and label it part-to-part or part-to-whole.
Students hold up boards. Then one student reads the answer aloud in words using ‘for every’.
Go through all five items together, fixing mistakes as they appear.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:
1. A bag has 4 red marbles and 6 blue marbles. Red to blue. Answer: 4:6, part-to-part.
2. Same bag. Red to all marbles. Answer: 4:10, part-to-whole.
3. A team has 7 girls and 5 boys. Boys to girls. Answer: 5:7, part-to-part.
4. Same team. Girls to all players. Answer: 7:12, part-to-whole.
5. A shelf has 8 math books and 3 science books. Science books to all books. Answer: 3:11, part-to-whole.
Watch for 4:6 reduced; accept it and say simplifying comes later in the course.

segments.title: Same numbers, different ratio
segments.description:
Pose this to pairs: a pencil case holds 2 pens and 5 pencils. Anna says the ratio is 2:5 and Ben says it is 5:2.
Pairs decide who is right and what each ratio would mean in words.
Take two or three pair responses, then ask how they could tell from the words which number goes first.
segments.teacherNotes: Both are right, depending on the question. 2:5 is pens to pencils; 5:2 is pencils to pens. Neither is a part-to-whole ratio, since the whole is 7. Push students to say ‘pens to pencils’ aloud. Key rule: the first word names the first number.

segments.title: Exit ticket on paper
segments.description:
Students work alone and silently on a half sheet of paper. Remove the board examples before they start.
They answer one question with three parts about a class of pets.
Collect the sheets at the end of the segment to see who needs more practice.
segments.teacherNotes: Question: A pet store window has 5 puppies and 3 kittens. (a) Write the ratio of puppies to kittens in all three forms. (b) Write the ratio of kittens to all animals as a:b. (c) Is the ratio in (b) part-to-part or part-to-whole? Answers: (a) 5 puppies for every 3 kittens; 5:3; 5 to 3. (b) 3:8. (c) Part-to-whole. Do not grade this ticket.

segments.title: Say it back
segments.description:
Return to the fruit bowl. Ask students to give one part-to-part and one part-to-whole ratio for it in the form they prefer.
Restate that the order of the words decides the order of the numbers.
Preview that later in the course they will build tables of equal ratios.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected answers: 3:2 (apples to bananas) and 3:5 (apples to all fruit), or the bananas versions 2:3 and 2:5. Use the exit tickets to choose a few students to review at the start of next time.

keyIdeas: A ratio compares two quantities. 3 apples for every 2 bananas compares the amounts in a fruit bowl.
One ratio can be written three ways: in words (3 apples for every 2 bananas), as a:b (3:2) and as a to b (3 to 2).
A part-to-part ratio compares one group with another group, such as apples to bananas (3:2).
A part-to-whole ratio compares one group with the total, such as apples to all fruit (3:5).
Order matters. Apples to bananas is 3:2, but bananas to apples is 2:3.

vocabulary.definition: A comparison of two quantities, such as 3 apples for every 2 bananas.
Words used to describe a ratio, as in 3 apples for every 2 bananas.
The colon notation for a ratio, read ‘a to b’. For example, 3:2.
A ratio that compares one group with another group, such as apples to bananas.
A ratio that compares one group with the total of all groups, such as apples to all fruit.
The total of all the parts. In a bowl of 3 apples and 2 bananas, the whole is 5 fruits.

study.overview: A ratio compares two quantities. Today you learned to write a ratio in words, as a:b and as a to b. You also learned to tell a part-to-part ratio from a part-to-whole ratio, and why the order of the numbers matters. In the fruit bowl with 3 apples and 2 bananas, the ratio of apples to bananas is 3:2.

points.heading: Three ways to write one ratio
points.explanation: One ratio can be written in words, as a:b, or as a to b. All three mean the same thing. For the fruit bowl, apples to bananas is: 3 apples for every 2 bananas; 3:2; 3 to 2. Write it as a:b or a to b, not as a fraction like 3/2. Try it: a pet store window has 4 puppies and 1 kitten. Puppies to kittens is 4 puppies for every 1 kitten; 4:1; 4 to 1.

points.heading: Part-to-part and part-to-whole
points.explanation: A part-to-part ratio compares one group with another group. Apples to bananas is part-to-part: 3:2. A part-to-whole ratio compares one group with the total. Apples to all fruit is part-to-whole. The whole is 3 + 2 = 5 pieces of fruit, so the ratio is 3:5, not 3:2. A common mistake is to forget to add the parts to find the whole. Another example: a bag has 4 red marbles and 6 blue marbles. Red to blue is 4:6, which is part-to-part. Red to all marbles is 4:10, which is part-to-whole.

points.heading: Order matters
points.explanation: The first word names the first number. Apples to bananas is 3:2, but bananas to apples is 2:3. These are different ratios because they put the groups in a different order. Think of a pencil case with 2 pens and 5 pencils. Pens to pencils is 2:5. Pencils to pens is 5:2. Both are correct, but they answer different questions. Always read the words first and write the numbers in that order.

l_8b6942413961.title: Equivalent ratios and ratio tables
l_8b6942413961.summary: Students build ratio tables by multiplying both quantities by the same number and use them to find missing values in equivalent ratios.

segments.title: Back to the fruit bowl
segments.description:
Draw the fruit bowl from last time with 3 apples and 2 bananas.
Students write the ratio of apples to bananas as a:b on a mini whiteboard and hold it up.
Then ask: if we put out a second identical bowl, how many apples and how many bananas are there altogether?
Take two or three answers and leave them on the board.
segments.teacherNotes: Use exit tickets from last time to pick two or three students to explain 5:3 and 3:8 aloud. Expect 3:2, then 6 apples and 4 bananas. Drawings only, no real food. Do not write the ratio as a fraction.

segments.title: Building a ratio table
segments.description:
Draw a two-row table: apples on top, bananas below. Start with 1 bowl: 3 apples, 2 bananas.
Fill in 2 bowls (6 and 4), 3 bowls (9 and 6) and 4 bowls (12 and 8), drawing a ×2, ×3 or ×4 arrow over both rows each time.
Name the columns equivalent ratios: they describe the same comparison with different amounts.
Show that 3:2, 6:4, 9:6 and 12:8 are all read as apples to bananas. Then ask: 15 apples, how many bananas? Find the multiplier together (3 × 5 = 15), so bananas are 2 × 5 = 10.
segments.teacherNotes: Stress: the same number multiplies both rows. Common mistake: adding 3 to both (3:2 to 6:5). Draw bowls beside the table so students see each bowl repeated. Name the multiplier aloud each time.

segments.title: Fill in the missing value
segments.description:
Show one ratio at a time, each with a missing value. Students draw a two-row table and write the multiplier arrow.
They write the missing number on a mini whiteboard and hold it up.
One student explains the multiplier aloud before the next item.
Go through all four items together, fixing mistakes as they appear.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:
1. Red to blue marbles is 4:6. Find ?: 12:? Answer: ×3, so 12:18.
2. Pens to pencils is 2:5. Find 10:? Answer: ×5, so 10:25.
3. Boys to girls is 5:7. Find ?:21. Answer: ×3, so 15:21.
4. Puppies to kittens is 5:3. Find 20:? Answer: ×4, so 20:12.
Item 3 needs 21 ÷ 7 to find the multiplier.

segments.title: Are these ratios equivalent?
segments.description:
Show two ratios side by side. Pairs decide whether they are equivalent and must show the multiplier that proves it.
If the ratios are not equivalent, pairs say which number breaks the pattern.
Take two or three pair answers for each item, then ask what the quick test is.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:
1. 3:2 and 12:8. Yes, ×4 both.
2. 3:2 and 6:5. No: 3 × 2 = 6 but 2 × 2 = 4, not 5. Addition fails.
3. 2:5 and 6:15. Yes, ×3 both.
4. 5:3 and 15:10. No: ×3 gives 15:9.
Key rule: one multiplier must work for both numbers.

segments.title: Exit ticket: tables and tests
segments.description:
Students work alone and silently on a half sheet of paper. Remove the board examples before they start.
They answer one question with three parts about a trail mix recipe.
Collect the sheets at the end of the segment to see who needs more practice.
segments.teacherNotes:
Question: A trail mix uses 4 cups of oats for every 3 cups of raisins. (a) Complete the ratio table: oats 4, 8, ?, 20; raisins 3, ?, 9, ?. (b) Is 12:9 equivalent to 4:3? Show why. (c) Is 10:6 equivalent to 4:3? Show why.
Answers: (a) oats 12; raisins 6 and 15. (b) Yes, ×3 both. (c) No: 4 × 2.5 = 10 but 3 × 2.5 = 7.5, not 6. Not graded; no real food.

segments.title: Say it back
segments.description:
Ask students to complete aloud: equivalent ratios are made by multiplying both numbers by the same number.
Return to the fruit bowl table and ask one student to give a new column.
Preview that next time they will draw pictures of ratios called tape diagrams.
segments.teacherNotes: Use the exit tickets to choose a few students to check in on at the start of next time.

keyIdeas: Equivalent ratios describe the same comparison with different amounts. 3 apples for every 2 bananas, 6 apples for every 4 bananas and 9 apples for every 6 bananas are all equivalent.
A ratio table lists equivalent ratios in columns. To move from one column to another, multiply both quantities by the same number.
To find a missing value, work out the number that takes the known quantity to its new value, then multiply the other quantity by that same number.

To decide whether two ratios are equivalent, check whether one multiplier turns both numbers of the first ratio into both numbers of the second. Adding the same number to both quantities does not keep the ratio the same.

study.overview: Equivalent ratios describe the same comparison using different amounts. A ratio table lists them side by side, and one multiplier links the columns. This guide shows how to build a table, find a missing value and test whether two ratios are equivalent.

points.heading: Equivalent ratios and ratio tables
points.explanation: Equivalent ratios describe the same comparison with different amounts. Think of a fruit bowl with 3 apples and 2 bananas. Two identical bowls hold 6 apples and 4 bananas. Three bowls hold 9 apples and 6 bananas. So 3:2, 6:4 and 9:6 are all equivalent, and each is read as apples to bananas. A ratio table puts these ratios in columns, with apples in the top row and bananas in the bottom row. Bowls 1, 2, 3 and 4 give apples 3, 6, 9, 12 and bananas 2, 4, 6, 8. To move from one column to the next, multiply both rows by the same number. Going from 1 bowl to 4 bowls is ×4: 3 × 4 = 12 and 2 × 4 = 8.

points.heading: Finding a missing value
points.explanation: To find a missing value, first find the multiplier for the quantity you know. Then multiply the other quantity by that same number. Example: apples to bananas is 3:2, and there are 15 apples. Ask what number times 3 gives 15. It is 5, because 3 × 5 = 15. Now multiply the bananas by 5: 2 × 5 = 10. So 15 apples go with 10 bananas, and 15:10 is equivalent to 3:2. Sometimes you must divide to find the multiplier. Suppose the ratio of cats to dogs is 2:3 and there are 12 dogs. The multiplier is 12 ÷ 3 = 4, so there are 2 × 4 = 8 cats. Drawing a two-row table and writing the multiplier arrow over both rows helps you keep track.

points.heading: Deciding whether two ratios are equivalent
points.explanation: Two ratios are equivalent if one multiplier turns both numbers of the first ratio into both numbers of the second. Example: are 3:2 and 12:8 equivalent? Since 3 × 4 = 12 and 2 × 4 = 8, the same multiplier works for both. Yes, they are equivalent. Now try 2:5 and 6:15. Here 2 × 3 = 6 and 5 × 3 = 15, so they are equivalent too. Next, are 3:2 and 6:5 equivalent? 3 × 2 = 6, but 2 × 2 = 4, not 5. No single multiplier works, so they are not equivalent. The number 5 breaks the pattern. Be careful with a common mistake. Adding 3 to both numbers of 3:2 gives 6:5, but adding the same number to both quantities does not keep the ratio the same. Only multiplying both by the same number does.

points.heading: Quick check for yourself
points.explanation: Remember this rule: equivalent ratios are made by multiplying both numbers by the same number. To test yourself, make up a ratio such as 5 muffins for every 4 cookies. Build a ratio table with three more columns, and write the multiplier over each one. Then write one pair of ratios that is equivalent and one pair that is not, and explain which number breaks the pattern. Next time you will draw pictures of ratios called tape diagrams.

l_01f811c5bb70.title: Tape diagrams for ratio problems
l_01f811c5bb70.summary: Students draw tape diagrams to show ratios and solve problems that give a part, the whole or a difference between quantities.

segments.title: From the table to a picture
segments.description:
Redraw the fruit bowl ratio table from last time on the board: apples 3, 6, 9 and bananas 2, 4, 6.
Students write the apples to bananas ratio for each column as a:b on a mini whiteboard and hold it up.
Ask what stays the same in every column, then say that today they will draw a ratio as a picture called a tape diagram.
segments.teacherNotes: Use last time’s exit tickets to pick two students to say why 12:9 is equivalent to 4:3. Expect 3:2, 6:4 and 9:6. These ratios are equivalent: multiplying both quantities in 3:2 by 2 gives 6:4, and multiplying both by 3 gives 9:6. Drawings only, no real food.

segments.title: Drawing a ratio as a tape diagram
segments.description:
Draw two rows of equal boxes for the fruit bowl: 3 boxes labeled apples, 2 boxes labeled bananas. Name each box a unit and stress that all boxes are the same size.
Bracket all 5 boxes to show the whole, and link it to the 3:5 part-to-whole ratio from earlier.
Then say each box stands for 4 fruit, label the boxes 4, and find 12 apples and 8 bananas, linking it to the ×4 column in the table.
Students copy the diagram and the labels.
segments.teacherNotes: Common mistake: boxes drawn in different sizes, or the order of the rows swapped. Read the order from the words: the first quantity named is the top row. Do not write the ratio as a fraction.

segments.title: Draw it
segments.description:
Show four ratios one at a time. Students draw a tape diagram for each on a mini whiteboard and hold it up.
One student explains how many boxes each row has and why.
Go through all four together, fixing mistakes as they appear.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:
1. Red to blue marbles, 4:6. Top row 4 boxes, bottom row 6 boxes.
2. Pens to pencils, 2:5. 2 boxes over 5 boxes.
3. Boys to girls, 5:7. 5 boxes over 7 boxes.
4. Puppies to kittens, 5:3. 5 boxes over 3 boxes.
Check equal box sizes.

segments.title: Finding the value of one unit
segments.description:
Pose: apples to bananas is 3:2 and there are 20 fruit in all. Draw 5 boxes in total, divide 20 by 5 to get 4 for one unit, then label 12 apples and 8 bananas.
Pose: apples to bananas is 3:2 and there are 15 apples. Match 15 to the 3 apple boxes, so one unit is 5 and bananas are 2 × 5 = 10.
Students write the same steps beside each diagram: draw, match the given number to its boxes, find one unit, then answer.
segments.teacherNotes: Common mistake: dividing 20 by 3 because only the apple boxes are in mind. Ask which boxes the given number covers. A given whole covers all the boxes; a given part covers only its own. Check answers by adding: 12 + 8 = 20.

segments.title: Solve with a tape diagram

study.overview: Today you learned to draw a ratio as a tape diagram and to use the picture to solve problems. A tape diagram shows each quantity as a row of equal boxes. Each box is one unit. When a problem gives you a number, you decide which boxes that number covers, find the value of one unit, and then answer the question.

points.heading: Draw a ratio as equal boxes
points.explanation: A tape diagram shows a ratio as a row of boxes for each quantity. Every box is the same size, and each box is one unit. The numbers in the ratio tell you how many boxes each quantity gets. Read the order from the words: the first quantity named is the top row. Example: apples to bananas is 3:2. Draw 3 equal boxes for apples on top and 2 equal boxes for bananas underneath. All the boxes together are the whole: 3 + 2 = 5 boxes. Common mistakes are drawing boxes of different sizes and swapping the rows.

points.heading: Give each box a value
points.explanation: The boxes show how the quantities compare. To find real amounts, decide what one box is worth. In the fruit bowl, suppose each box stands for 4 fruit. Write 4 in every box. Apples are 3 boxes, so 3 × 4 = 12 apples. Bananas are 2 boxes, so 2 × 4 = 8 bananas. This is the same as the ×4 column in a ratio table. Now the picture and the table match.

points.heading: Match the number you are given to its boxes
points.explanation: To solve a ratio problem, first draw the diagram. Then ask which boxes the given number covers. Divide that number by the number of boxes it covers to get the value of one unit. Then multiply to find the other quantities. Example with a given whole: apples to bananas is 3:2 and there are 20 fruit in all. The whole covers all 5 boxes, so one unit is 20 ÷ 5 = 4. Apples are 3 × 4 = 12 and bananas are 2 × 4 = 8. Check by adding: 12 + 8 = 20. Example with a given part: apples to bananas is 3:2 and there are 15 apples. The 15 covers only the 3 apple boxes, so one unit is 15 ÷ 3 = 5. Bananas are 2 × 5 = 10. Do not divide 20 by 3 in the first problem. The 20 is the whole, so it covers all the boxes.

points.heading: Parts, wholes and differences
points.explanation: A problem can give you a part, the whole or a difference. A part fills the boxes of one quantity. A whole fills all the boxes. A difference fills only the extra boxes that one quantity has. Example with a difference: puppies to kittens is 5:3, and there are 8 more puppies than kittens. Puppies have 5 boxes and kittens have 3, so puppies have 2 extra boxes. Those 2 boxes stand for 8, so one unit is 8 ÷ 2 = 4. Puppies are 5 × 4 = 20 and kittens are 3 × 4 = 12. Check: 20 − 12 = 8. A good routine is to draw the boxes, match the number you are given to its boxes, find the value of one unit, and then answer in a sentence.

segments.title: In-class quiz: ratio language, tables and tape diagrams

Clear the board and the screen. Hand out the quiz and tell students to work alone and silently.
Students answer four written questions on ratio language, ratio tables and tape diagrams.
Collect every paper at the end of the time. This quiz counts toward the in-class quizzes part of the course grade.
segments.teacherNotes:
Quiz, 10 points.
Q1 (2): A garden has 6 tulips and 9 daisies. (a) Write tulips to daisies as a:b. 6:9 (1). (b) Write tulips to all flowers as a:b and say part-to-part or part-to-whole. 6:15, part-to-whole (1).
Q2 (2): A parking lot has cars and trucks in the ratio 3:7. Say it with ‘for every’ (3 cars for every 7 trucks, 1). Write trucks to cars as a:b (7:3, 1).
Q3 (3): Paint mix, blue to white. Complete the table: blue 2, 6, ?, 14; white 5, ?, 25, ?. Answers: 15 (1), 10 (1), 35 (1).
Q4 (3): Stars to hearts on stickers is 5:2, with 21 stickers in all. Draw a tape diagram with 5 boxes over 2 boxes (1). One unit is 21 ÷ 7 = 3 (1). 15 stars and 6 hearts (1).
Accept 6/9 style answers only if the order is right; note it, do not deduct for ratio form.

Ask students how many words Mia types in 1 minute. Take two or three answers and show the arrow ÷2 over both rows to get 30 words in 1 minute.
Say that this column, with 1 in the bottom row, is the one we will study today.
segments.teacherNotes: Expect some students to say 30 right away, others to guess 58. Ask which number divides both rows. Use last time’s tape diagram idea: 2 boxes, each box is 30 words. Link back to the multiplier idea, now dividing.

segments.title: Rates and the words per and for each
segments.description:
Write 12 miles in 3 hours. Say that when the two quantities have different units, the ratio is called a rate.
Write the rate as 12 miles to 3 hours. Then draw a ratio table with 12 and 3 and a ÷3 arrow to 4 miles in 1 hour.
Teach two ways to say the unit rate: 4 miles per hour and 4 miles for each hour. Students copy both sentences and the new terms rate, unit rate and per.
segments.teacherNotes: Stress: per means for each 1. Contrast with earlier ratios like 3:2 where both quantities were fruit; here the units differ, so always write the units. Common mistake: leaving out units, writing just 4. Do not write the rate as a fraction yet.

segments.title: Finding a unit rate by division
segments.description:
Show that the table step is a division: 12 ÷ 3 = 4, so the unit rate is 4 miles per hour. Ask which number goes first in the division.
Pose: a bike rider goes 20 miles in 4 hours. Students find the unit rate on a mini whiteboard and hold it up.
Pose: a store sells 3 notebooks for $6. Students find dollars per notebook, then write the answer in a sentence with per and again with for each.
Students copy the rule: divide the first quantity by the quantity that comes after per.
segments.teacherNotes: Answers: 20 ÷ 4 = 5 miles per hour. $6 ÷ 3 = $2 per notebook; $2 for each notebook. Common mistake: dividing 3 ÷ 6 or 4 ÷ 20. Ask: per what? That quantity is the divisor. Check by multiplying back: 5 × 4 = 20.

segments.title: Find it and say it
segments.description:
Show four rates one at a time. Students find the unit rate on a mini whiteboard and write one sentence with per or for each.
Students hold up boards. One student reads the sentence aloud before the next item.
Go through all four items together, fixing mistakes as they appear.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:
1. $12 for 4 pounds of grapes. $3 per pound.
2. 45 pages in 3 hours. 15 pages per hour.
3. 30 meters in 6 seconds. 5 meters per second.
4. 18 cups of juice for 9 children. 2 cups for each child.
Watch for missing units and for dividing in the wrong order.

segments.title: Exit ticket: the faucet
segments.description:
Students work alone and silently on a half sheet of paper. Remove all board examples before they start.
They answer one question with three parts about a faucet filling a tank. Collect the sheets at the end of the segment to see who needs more practice.
segments.teacherNotes:
Question: A faucet fills 36 gallons in 4 minutes. (a) Find the unit rate. (b) Write the rate in a sentence using per. (c) Write it again using for each.
Answers: (a) 36 ÷ 4 = 9 gallons per minute. (b) The faucet fills 9 gallons per minute. (c) The faucet fills 9 gallons for each minute.
Use the sheets to choose students to check in with next time.

segments.title: Say it back
segments.description:
Ask students to complete aloud: a unit rate tells how much for 1 of something. Ask which number I divide by.
Return to the 12 miles in 3 hours table and ask for the unit rate in both wordings.
Preview that next time they will use unit rates to solve bigger problems.
segments.teacherNotes: Look for students who still divide by the quantity before per. Review them first next time.

keyIdeas: A rate is a ratio that compares two quantities with different units, such as miles and hours, or dollars and pounds.
A unit rate tells how much of the first quantity there is for 1 of the second quantity. 12 miles in 3 hours is 4 miles per hour.
To find a unit rate, divide the first quantity by the second quantity. The quantity after ‘per’ is the one you divide by.
A rate can be said with ‘per’ or ‘for each’. 4 miles per hour and 4 miles for each hour mean the same thing.
A unit rate is the ratio table column where the second quantity is 1. Dividing both numbers by the same multiplier gets you there.

vocabulary.definition: A ratio that compares two quantities with different units, such as 12 miles in 3 hours.
A rate that tells how much of one quantity there is for 1 of the other, such as 4 miles per hour.
A word that means ‘for each 1'. In 4 miles per hour, per hour means for each 1 hour. To find miles per hour, divide the number of miles by the number of hours.

study.overview: Today you learned that a rate compares two quantities with different units, such as miles and hours or dollars and notebooks. You learned how to find a unit rate by dividing, and how to say a rate with the words per and for each. Use this guide to review the ideas and try the examples again on your own.

points.heading: A rate compares different units
points.explanation: A ratio can compare two quantities with the same kind of unit, like fruit to fruit. A rate is a ratio that compares two quantities with different units. For example, 12 miles in 3 hours compares miles to hours, so it is a rate. Always write the units. If you write just 4 and leave out the units, nobody knows what the number means.

points.heading: A unit rate has 1 in the second place
points.explanation: A unit rate tells how much of the first quantity there is for 1 of the second quantity. In a ratio table, it is the column where the bottom number is 1. Start with 60 words typed in 2 minutes. Divide both rows by 2 and you get 30 words in 1 minute. The unit rate is 30 words per minute. Dividing both numbers by the same number keeps the ratio equivalent, just as multiplying both did before.

points.heading: Divide by the quantity after per
points.explanation: To find a unit rate, divide the first quantity by the second quantity. The quantity that comes after per is the one you divide by. For 12 miles in 3 hours, the rate is 12 ÷ 3 = 4 miles per hour. A common mistake is dividing in the wrong order, such as 3 ÷ 6 for 3 notebooks that cost $6. Ask yourself: per what? Here it is dollars per notebook, so you divide by 3 notebooks: $6 ÷ 3 = $2 per notebook. Check by multiplying back. A bike rider who goes 5 miles each hour for 4 hours goes 5 × 4 = 20 miles, which matches 20 miles in 4 hours.

points.heading: Say a rate with per or for each
points.explanation: Per means for each 1. So 4 miles per hour and 4 miles for each hour mean exactly the same thing. You can say the notebook rate both ways: the notebooks cost $2 per notebook, or $2 for each notebook. Try this one on your own: 45 pages in 3 hours. Divide the pages by the hours, then write a sentence with per and another with for each.

l_00332a8fefab.summary: Students use unit price, speed and other unit rates to compare deals, find costs and calculate distances and times.

segments.title: Back to unit rates
segments.description:
Show three rates one at a time. Students find the unit rate on a mini whiteboard and hold it up.
One student reads the answer aloud as a sentence with per or for each.
Remind the class that the quantity after per is the one we divide by.
segments.teacherNotes: Items: 1. 24 miles in 6 hours: 4 miles per hour. 2. $15 for 5 pounds of apples: $3 per pound. 3. 56 pages in 7 hours: 8 pages for each hour. Check units. Use last time’s exit tickets to call on students who divided by the wrong quantity. Hand back last time’s quiz papers as students arrive.

segments.title: Which is the better buy?
segments.description:
Pose: Store A sells 4 pounds of rice for $6. Store B sells 10 pounds of rice for $14. Ask which is cheaper and take two or three guesses.
Find dollars per pound for each store by dividing the cost by the pounds. Name this rate the unit price and write: the lower unit price is the better buy.
Check with a ratio table: 20 pounds costs $30 at Store A and $28 at Store B. Students copy the two unit prices and the rule.
segments.teacherNotes: Answers: A is $6 ÷ 4 = $1.50 per pound. B is $14 ÷ 10 = $1.40 per pound. B is the better buy. Common mistake: choosing A because $6 is less than $14. Ask: do we get the same amount of rice? Always write the unit with the price.

segments.title: Compare the deals
segments.description:
Show four pairs of deals one at a time. Pairs find both unit prices and say which is the better buy.
Pairs must write each unit price with its unit.
After each item, one pair explains how they decided. Fix mistakes as they appear.
segments.teacherNotes: Items and answers: 1. Juice: 6 bottles for $9 or 8 bottles for $10. $1.50 vs $1.25 per bottle, second. 2. Granola bars: 5 for $4 or 20 for $17. $0.80 vs $0.85 per bar, first. 3. Grapes: 3 pounds for $6 or 5 pounds for $10. Both $2 per pound, same deal. 4. Pencils: 12 for $3 or 20 for $4. $0.25 vs $0.20, second. Bigger pack is not always cheaper.

segments.title: Speed, distance and time
segments.description:
Say that speed is a unit rate: a cyclist who rides 15 miles per hour goes 15 miles in 1 hour. Draw a ratio table with 1 hour and 15 miles, then multiply both rows by 3 to find the distance in 3 hours.
Ask how long the cyclist needs to ride 60 miles. Divide 60 by 15 to get 4 hours, and show it on the table.
Pose: a train goes 180 miles in 3 hours. Find its speed, then how far it goes in 5 hours. Students copy: distance = speed × time, and time = distance ÷ speed.
segments.teacherNotes: Answers: 15 × 3 = 45 miles. 60 ÷ 15 = 4 hours. Train: 180 ÷ 3 = 60 miles per hour; 60 × 5 = 300 miles. Common mistake: multiplying when finding time. Ask: what does the table’s multiplier have to be? Check by multiplying back.

segments.title: Solve it with a rate
segments.description:
Pairs solve four problems on paper. For each one they draw a ratio table, find the unit rate or the multiplier, and write the answer in a sentence with units.
After each problem, one pair shows its table and says what they divided or multiplied.
Finish by asking which problems asked for a distance and which for a time.
segments.teacherNotes: Items and answers: 1. A car travels 55 miles per hour. How far in 4 hours? 220 miles. 2. A bus goes 150 miles in 3 hours. Speed? 50 miles per hour. How far in 5 hours? 250 miles. 3. A hiker walks 3 miles per hour. How long to walk 9 miles? 3 hours. 4. A train goes 80 miles per hour. How long to go 400 miles? 5 hours.

segments.title: Exit ticket: shops and trips
segments.description:
Students work alone and silently on a half sheet of paper. Remove all board examples before they start.
They answer one question with three parts about two potato prices and a train trip.
Collect the sheets at the end of the segment to see who needs more practice.
segments.teacherNotes: Question: Fresh Market sells 6 pounds of potatoes for $9. Corner Shop sells 10 pounds for $13. (a) Find the unit price at each shop. (b) Which is the better buy? (c) A train goes 90 miles per hour. How long does it take to go 270 miles? Answers: (a) $1.50 per pound; $1.30 per pound. (b) Corner Shop, lower unit price. (c) 270 ÷ 90 = 3 hours.

segments.title: Say it back
segments.description:
Ask students to complete aloud: to find the better buy, I find each unit price and choose the lower one.
Ask which operation finds a distance and which finds a time.
Preview that next time they will meet percent, a rate per 100.
segments.teacherNotes: Use the exit tickets to choose a few students to check in with at the start of next time. Look for comparing total prices and for multiplying when the problem asks for a time.

keyIdeas: A unit price is a unit rate that tells the cost for 1 item or 1 unit of measure, such as dollars per pound. To find it, divide the cost by the amount.
To choose the better buy, find the unit price of each deal and compare them. The lower unit price is the better buy. Comparing total prices does not work when the amounts are different.
Speed is a unit rate: the distance traveled in 1 unit of time, such as 55 miles per hour. Distance = speed × time.
To find a time, divide the distance by the speed. A ratio table with 1 hour in one column helps you see which operation to use.

vocabulary.definition: The cost of 1 item or 1 unit of measure, such as $1.50 per pound. It is a unit rate.
The deal with the lower unit price, because you pay less for each unit.
A unit rate that tells the distance traveled in 1 unit of time, such as 55 miles per hour.

study.overview: A unit rate tells you the amount for 1 of something, such as dollars for 1 pound or miles for 1 hour. In this lesson you used unit rates to compare deals and to solve speed, distance and time problems. The main idea is simple: find the unit rate first, then compare it or use it.

points.heading: Unit price tells the cost of 1
points.explanation: A unit price is a unit rate. It tells the cost for 1 item or 1 unit of measure, such as dollars per pound. To find it, divide the cost by the amount. Example: $15 for 5 pounds of apples is $15 ÷ 5 = $3 per pound. Always write the unit with the price. The quantity after per is the one you divide by.

points.heading: Compare unit prices to choose the better buy
points.explanation: To choose the better buy, find the unit price of each deal and compare them. The lower unit price is the better buy. Do not compare total prices, because the amounts are different. Example: Store A sells 4 pounds of rice for $6, and Store B sells 10 pounds for $14. Store A is $6 ÷ 4 = $1.50 per pound. Store B is $14 ÷ 10 = $1.40 per pound. Store B is the better buy, even though $14 is more than $6. A ratio table agrees: 20 pounds costs $30 at Store A and $28 at Store B. A bigger pack is not always cheaper, and sometimes two deals have the same unit price. Always check.

points.heading: Speed is a unit rate: find distance
points.explanation: Speed is the distance traveled in 1 unit of time, such as 55 miles per hour. To find a distance, use distance = speed × time. Example: a cyclist rides 15 miles per hour. In a ratio table, 1 hour matches 15 miles. Multiply both by 3, and 3 hours matches 15 × 3 = 45 miles. If you only know the distance and the time, divide to find the speed first. A train that goes 180 miles in 3 hours travels 180 ÷ 3 = 60 miles per hour. Then in 5 hours it goes 60 × 5 = 300 miles.

points.heading: Divide to find a time
points.explanation: To find a time, divide the distance by the speed: time = distance ÷ speed. Example: how long does the cyclist need to ride 60 miles at 15 miles per hour? 60 ÷ 15 = 4 hours. Do not multiply when the problem asks for a time. A ratio table with 1 hour in one column helps you see which operation to use. Ask what the multiplier has to be. Then check by multiplying back: 15 × 4 = 60 miles. Write your answer as a sentence with units.

study.overview: A percent is a rate per 100. When you see 35%, think “35 for every 100.” Today you saw that a percent can be shown on a 100-grid, written as a fraction or decimal, and marked on a double number line. These notes go over each idea with the examples from class.

points.heading: Percent means per 100
points.explanation: The word percent means per 100, in the same way that per hour means for each hour. On a 100-grid, the whole grid is always 100 squares. The shaded squares tell you the percent. If 35 squares are shaded, then 35 out of every 100 squares are shaded. That is 35 percent, written 35%. If 8 squares are shaded, that is 8 per 100, or 8%. A common mistake is to count the shaded squares as the whole. The whole is always the 100 squares.

points.heading: Write a percent as a fraction and a decimal
points.explanation: A percent is a fraction with denominator 100. So 35% is 35/100. You can simplify it the way you did with ratio tables: divide both rows by the same number. Divide 35 and 100 by 5 to get 7 and 20, so 35% = 7/20. As a decimal, 35% is 0.35. Watch out for 3.5 and 0.035, which are not right. Check with the grid: 35 squares out of 100 is 0.35 of the grid. Another example is 50%. It is 50/100, which simplifies to 1/2, and the decimal is 0.5.

points.heading: Mark a percent on a double number line
points.explanation: A double number line lines up percents with amounts out of 100. The top line shows percents and the bottom line shows squares. 0% sits above 0, and 100% sits above 100 squares, which is the whole grid. 50% sits halfway between, above 50. To mark 60%, find 60 on the bottom line and place 60% directly above it. Keep the tick marks evenly spaced. Folding a paper strip into quarters shows how equal spaces look. You can check any mark by shading the same number of squares on a grid. For example, 40% matches 40 shaded squares.

points.heading: Compare percents and check your work
points.explanation: A grid helps you compare percents. Which is more, 40% or 4%? Shade 40 squares on one grid and 4 squares on another. The 40% grid has far more shaded, so 40% is more. When you simplify a fraction, ask yourself whether it still means the same part of 100. For example, 20 squares shaded is 20%, which is 20/100 = 1/5. Next time you will use percents to find a part of other quantities.

Scale to an easy percent such as 10% or 5%, then scale to the percent you need. You can also go the other way: if you know a part and its percent, put the part under its percent and scale up to 100% to find the whole.

points.heading: Find a percent of a quantity with a ratio table
points.explanation: Draw a table with percents on the top row and amounts on the bottom row. Write 100% above the whole amount. Divide both rows to reach an easy percent, then multiply both rows to reach the percent you want. Example: a bag has 80 beads and 35% are blue. Put 100% above 80. Divide both rows by 20: 5% is above 80 ÷ 20 = 4 beads. Multiply both rows by 7: 35% is above 7 × 4 = 28 beads. Write a full sentence: 35% of 80 beads is 28 beads. A common mistake is to write 35 beads because 35% of 100 is 35. Ask yourself: is the whole 100 or 80? Here the whole is 80. You can also use 10% and then half of it to get 5%.

points.heading: Find the whole from a part and its percent
points.explanation: When you are given a part, do not put it under 100%. Put the part under its own percent, then scale both rows up to 100%. Example: 12 students in a club are 40% of the whole class. Write 40% above 12. Divide both rows by 4: 10% is above 3 students. Multiply both rows by 10: 100% is above 30 students. The class has 30 students. Another example: a $15 discount is 25% of the price. Multiply both rows by 4 to get 100% above $60, so the whole price is $60. A common mistake is to find 40% of 12 and get 4.8. Ask yourself: is 12 the whole or the part? Here 12 is the part.

points.heading: Check your answer by going the other way
points.explanation: After you find a whole, find the percent of that whole. You should get the part you started with. Example: you found that 12 students are 40% of a class of 30. Check by finding 40% of 30. 10% of 30 is 3, so 40% is 4 × 3 = 12. This matches the part, so the answer is correct. If the check does not match, look at your table. Make sure the whole is under 100% and the part is under its own percent.

Students clear their desks except for a pencil, an eraser and a ruler.
The board and screen are blank.

Students write their names and turn the paper over together.

segments.teacherNotes:
Test, 30 points. Walk the room silently; give no hints.
Q1 (3). A fruit bowl has 9 plums and 6 peaches. (a) Write the ratio of plums to peaches with a colon and with the word to. 9:6 and 9 to 6 (1). (b) Write the ratio of peaches to all the fruit in simplest form. 6 to 15 = 2 to 5 (2).
Q2 (4). Fruit punch uses 3 cups of juice for every 4 cups of sparkling water. (a) Complete the ratio table. Juice: 3, 6, ?, 21. Water: 4, ?, 20, ?. Answers: 8 (1), 15 (1), 28 (1). (b) How many cups of juice go with 36 cups of sparkling water? 27 cups (1).
Q3 (4). Maya and Leo share 45 stickers in the ratio 4 to 5, Maya to Leo. (a) Draw a tape diagram. Maya 4 equal boxes, Leo 5 equal boxes, 9 in all (1). (b) How many stickers in each box? 45 ÷ 9 = 5 (1). (c) How many stickers does each get? Maya 20 (1), Leo 25 (1).
Q4 (5). (a) A machine fills 54 bottles in 9 minutes. Find the unit rate. 6 bottles per minute (1). (b) Shop P sells 5 notebooks for $7.50. Shop Q sells 8 notebooks for $11.20. Find each unit price and say which is the better buy. P: $1.50 per notebook (1). Q: $1.40 per notebook (1). Q is the better buy because its unit price is lower (1). (c) How many bottles does the machine fill in 15 minutes? 90 bottles (1).
Q5 (3). A bus travels at 40 miles per hour. (a) How far does it go in 6 hours? 240 miles (1). (b) How long does it take to go 280 miles? 280 ÷ 40 = 7 hours (2: 1 for the operation, 1 for the answer with units).
Q6 (4). (a) 28 squares of a 100-grid are shaded. Write this as a percent and as a fraction in simplest form. 28% (1), 7/25 (1). (b) Write 85% as a fraction in simplest form and as a decimal. 17/20 (1), 0.85 (1).
Q7 (4). (a) Find 30% of 90 students. 10% is 9, so 30% is 27 students (2). (b) 18 is 25% of a number. Find the number. 25% is 18, so 100% is 72 (2).
Q8 (3). Sam says, ‘12% of 50 is 12, because 12% of 100 is 12.’ Explain the mistake and find the correct answer. The whole is 50, not 100 (1). 50 is half of 100, so halve the 12 (1). 12% of 50 is 6 (1).
Give full credit for any correct method, such as a table or a diagram. Take no points off for simplest form unless asked.

segments.teacherNotes: Check that every paper has a name. Do not discuss answers while others are still writing. Note any students who ran out of time or left Q8 blank, to follow up when marking.

keyIdeas: A ratio compares two quantities. It can be written as 9 to 6 or 9:6, and it can be simplified by dividing both parts by the same number.
Ratio tables and tape diagrams show equivalent ratios and split a total into equal parts, so one part can be found and scaled.
A unit rate compares a quantity to 1 unit, such as dollars per item or miles per hour. It is used to find unit prices, compare deals, and work out distance and time.
A percent is a rate per 100. It can be written as a fraction or decimal, and a ratio table with 100% above the whole finds a part or a whole.
A written explanation names the whole, says what was done to each row of the table, and checks that the answer makes sense.

study.overview: This unit covered how to compare quantities and scale them up or down. You used ratios, ratio tables, tape diagrams, unit rates and percents. Use this guide to review the main ideas and the habits that make your answers clear. Good written reasoning names the whole, says what you did, and checks that the answer makes sense.

points.heading: Ratios compare two quantities
points.explanation: A ratio compares two quantities. You can write it with the word to or with a colon. Suppose a basket has 12 apples and 8 pears. The ratio of apples to pears is 12 to 8, or 12:8. Divide both parts by the same number to simplify. Both 12 and 8 divide by 4, so the ratio is 3 to 2. Order matters. The ratio of pears to apples is 2 to 3.

points.heading: Ratio tables and tape diagrams show equivalent ratios
points.explanation: A ratio table keeps the same ratio by multiplying or dividing both rows by the same number. Suppose a paint mix uses 2 cans of blue for every 5 cans of white. Multiply both by 3 and you get 6 blue and 15 white. A tape diagram splits a total into equal parts. Suppose 40 marbles are shared in the ratio 3 to 5. Draw 3 boxes and 5 boxes, 8 in all. Each box holds 40 ÷ 8 = 5 marbles, so the shares are 15 and 25.

points.heading: Unit rates make comparing easy
points.explanation: A unit rate compares a quantity to 1 unit, such as dollars per item or miles per hour. Divide to find it. Suppose 4 pens cost $6. The unit price is $6 ÷ 4 = $1.50 per pen. To compare deals, find each unit price and choose the lower one. Unit rates also solve speed problems. Suppose a cyclist rides at 12 miles per hour. In 3 hours she goes 12 × 3 = 36 miles. To ride 60 miles takes 60 ÷ 12 = 5 hours.

points.heading: Percent is a rate per 100, and explanations need reasons
points.explanation: A percent is a rate per 100. So 60% means 60 out of 100, or 60/100 = 3/5, or 0.60. To find a part, use a ratio table with 100% above the whole. Suppose you want 20% of 150. Since 10% of 150 is 15, 20% is 30. Check the whole before you start. 20% of 50 is not the same as 20% of 150. When you explain, name the whole, say what you did to each row, and check that the answer is sensible. Clear reasoning matters more than length.

t_ed045be3b49a.prompt: A pencil case holds 2 pens and 5 pencils. Anna says the ratio is 2:5. Ben says it is 5:2. Who is right? Decide with your partner, then be ready to defend your answer to a pair who chose differently.
followUps: What question about the pencil case would make Anna’s 2:5 the right answer? What question would make Ben’s 5:2 the right answer?
How could you tell, just from the words, which number should go first?
Is either ratio a part-to-whole ratio? What would the whole be, and what ratio would you write for pens to all the items?

t_c39e6bba8a06.prompt: A student says: ‘For the fruit bowl with 3 apples and 2 bananas, the ratio of apples to all fruit is 3:2, because those are the two numbers in the picture.’ Do you agree? Argue for or against, and use the picture to support your claim.
followUps: What does the whole include here? How many pieces of fruit are in the bowl altogether?
What would 3:2 correctly compare? Say it aloud using the words ‘for every’.
How is a part-to-part ratio different from a part-to-whole ratio, and how can you tell which one a question is asking for?

t_2be3b3dc4fe5.prompt: A jar has 6 green beads and 4 yellow beads. Which choice gives the ratio of green beads to yellow beads in three forms?

choices.text: 4 green beads for every 6 yellow beads; 4:6; 4 to 6
6 green beads for every 10 beads; 6:10; 6 to 10
6 green beads for every 4 yellow beads; 6:4; 6 to 4
10 green beads for every 4 yellow beads; 10:4; 10 to 4

t_2be3b3dc4fe5.explanation: The order is green beads to yellow beads, so green beads come first in all three forms.

t_88af0c2e1de2.prompt: A class has 9 students who walk to school and 7 students who ride the bus. Write the ratio of walkers to bus riders in words, as a:b, and as a to b.
t_88af0c2e1de2.answer: 9 walkers for every 7 bus riders; 9:7; 9 to 7
t_88af0c2e1de2.explanation: Walkers are named first, so 9 is first in each form of the ratio.

t_eac3dc94f7d9.prompt: An aquarium has 5 goldfish and 3 guppies. What is the ratio of guppies to all fish, and what kind of ratio is it?
t_eac3dc94f7d9.explanation: There are 8 fish altogether. The ratio compares the 3 guppies with all 8 fish.

t_cc8d92590156.prompt: If a box has 4 toy cars and 6 toy trucks, then 6:4 describes trucks to cars.
t_cc8d92590156.explanation: Trucks are named first, so their count, 6, comes first in the ratio.

t_6da3d7632136.prompt: A box has 8 striped buttons and 5 plain buttons. Which choice gives the ratio of plain buttons to all buttons and names its type?
t_6da3d7632136.explanation: There are 13 buttons altogether. The ratio compares the 5 plain buttons with the whole group of 13.

t_62d60141c002.prompt: Two students make ratio tables for 3 apples to 2 bananas. Maya’s next column is 6 apples and 5 bananas, because she added 3 to the apples and 3 to the bananas. Leo’s next column is 6 apples and 4 bananas. Who is right? Argue for one answer, then try to convince someone who picked the other.
followUps: If you put out a second identical bowl, what happens to the apples? What happens to the bananas? How does that show which column is right?
Maya’s column keeps the difference between apples and bananas the same as before. Why does that not keep the comparison the same?
What would you say to Maya to help her see where her thinking breaks, without just telling her the rule?

t_e6ed8f1dca35.prompt: A friend says: ‘To check if two ratios are equivalent, I just see whether the first number grew by the same amount as the second.’ Is that a good quick test? Decide whether you agree, disagree or only partly agree, and use 3:2 and 6:5, and 3:2 and 12:8, to support your view.
followUps: For 3:2 and 12:8, find the multiplier for the first numbers and for the second numbers. What do you notice?
What does ‘the same amount’ mean in your friend’s test: added, or multiplied? How can you reword the test so it always works?
Can you make up a pair of ratios that fools the friend’s test but is not equivalent? Explain how you built it.

t_883e20bc5fc0.prompt: A ratio table begins with 6 red beads for every 5 blue beads. If the red-bead count changes to 18, what blue-bead count keeps the ratio equivalent?
t_883e20bc5fc0.explanation: The red-bead count is multiplied by 3, so the blue-bead count must also be multiplied by 3: 5 × 3 = 15.

t_ba0904231706.prompt: Which pair of ratios is equivalent?
t_ba0904231706.explanation: Multiplying both numbers in 4:7 by 3 gives 12:21.

t_86923c21e414.prompt: A ratio table has 8 green tiles for every 3 yellow tiles. Which column gives an equivalent ratio with 24 green tiles?
t_86923c21e414.explanation: The green-tile count is multiplied by 3. Multiplying 3 yellow tiles by 3 gives 9.

t_3739e003849f.prompt: The ratio of blue folders to red folders is 7:4. In an equivalent ratio, there are 21 blue folders. How many red folders are there?
t_3739e003849f.explanation: The blue-folder count is multiplied by 3, so multiply the red-folder count by 3 as well.

t_bcc78f13ab3f.prompt: The ratios 5:8 and 10:13 are equivalent because each number in the second ratio is 5 greater.
t_bcc78f13ab3f.explanation: Adding 5 to both numbers does not keep the ratio equivalent. Multiplying both numbers by the same number does.

t_d6de9a5f2716.prompt: Two students draw a tape diagram for apples to bananas as 3:2. One draws 3 boxes over 2 boxes, all the same size. The other draws 3 boxes over 2 boxes, but makes the apple boxes bigger because there are more apples. Which diagram is right? Argue for your choice and explain what each box means.
followUps: If the boxes can be different sizes, what would the diagram say about the ratio of apples to bananas in one box?
How does the idea that every box is one unit help you find 12 apples and 8 bananas when each box stands for 4 fruit?
Suppose someone swaps the rows and puts bananas on top. How can the words of the problem tell you which row goes first?

t_3e46bfd5de63.prompt: A problem says apples to bananas is 3:2 and gives the number 20. A classmate says, ‘Divide 20 by 3 to find one unit.’ Another says, ‘Divide 20 by 5.’ Who is right? Decide using the tape diagram. What would change if the problem said there are 15 apples instead of 20 fruit in all?
followUps: Which boxes does the number 20 cover? Which boxes does 15 cover when it is the number of apples?
How can you check your answer by adding the apples and bananas?
In the problem about puppies to kittens at 5:3 with 8 more puppies than kittens, what do the 2 extra boxes stand for, and why is 8 not the value of one unit?

t_9aa4787fa1ef.prompt: A ratio of shells to buttons is 4:3. Which description gives a correct tape diagram?

choices.text: 3 equal shells boxes above 4 equal buttons boxes
4 equal shells boxes above 3 equal buttons boxes
4 larger shells boxes above 3 smaller buttons boxes
4 equal buttons boxes above 3 equal shells boxes

t_9aa4787fa1ef.explanation: The first quantity named, shells, gets 4 equal boxes. Buttons get 3 equal boxes, and every box has the same size.

t_e91b5832b92c.prompt: For a ratio of flags to banners of 5:2, a tape diagram has 5 equal boxes for flags and 2 equal boxes for banners.
t_e91b5832b92c.explanation: The ratio numbers give the number of equal boxes for each quantity, in the order named.

t_8ea601319296.prompt: The ratio of red flags to yellow flags is 3:4. There are 42 flags in all. What is the value of one unit?
t_8ea601319296.explanation: The whole covers 3 + 4 = 7 boxes. Divide 42 flags by 7 boxes to find the value of one unit.

t_781b9e77c19b.prompt: Purple beads to green beads are in a ratio of 2:7. If there are 35 green beads, how many purple beads are there?
t_781b9e77c19b.explanation: The 35 green beads cover 7 boxes, so each box is worth 5 beads. The 2 purple boxes contain 2 × 5 = 10 beads.

t_cb79ec2d7e46.prompt: Cats to dogs are in a ratio of 6:4. If there are 10 more cats than dogs, the value of one unit is 10.
t_cb79ec2d7e46.explanation: The difference covers 6 − 4 = 2 boxes. If 2 boxes equal 10, one unit is 10 ÷ 2 = 5.

t_6493c3281050.prompt: Mia says, “A unit rate is just a division, so 12 miles in 3 hours can be 12 ÷ 3 or 3 ÷ 12. Both give a unit rate.” Do you agree? Decide with a partner, then be ready to defend your answer using the words per and for each.
followUps: What does 3 ÷ 12 tell you about the situation, and what units would you attach to it? Does it describe miles for each hour or something else?
How can you check a unit rate by multiplying back? Try 4 × 3 and then try 0.25 × 12. Which one gets you back to the numbers in the problem?
In the store problem, 3 notebooks for $6, how does the word after per tell you which number to divide by?

t_c391f7666226.prompt: A classmate writes only “4" as the answer to 12 miles in 3 hours and says, “The units are obvious, so we do not need to write them.” Should a unit rate always include its units? Argue for or against, using an example where leaving them out could cause confusion.
followUps: Look at 36 gallons in 4 minutes and 36 gallons in 4 gallons of paint. How could the bare number 9 mean different things? What does each unit tell the reader?
Is 4 miles per hour the same claim as 4 miles for each hour? What makes the two sentences mean the same thing?
How is a rate different from a ratio like 3:2 where both quantities are fruit? Why do the units matter more for a rate?

t_50bb709613cb.prompt: Store A sells 4 pounds of rice for $6. Store B sells 10 pounds of rice for $14. A classmate says, “Store A is the better buy because $6 is less than $14.” Do you agree? Decide where you stand, then convince a neighbor who disagrees with you.
followUps: Do we get the same amount of rice for $6 and for $14? Why does that matter when we compare?
What would we need to know or find so that comparing the two prices is fair?
Could comparing total prices ever work? What would have to be true about the amounts?

t_6480654fae9b.prompt: A bigger pack is always the cheaper deal per item. Is that true? Use the pencil packs (12 for $3 and 20 for $4) or the grapes (3 pounds for $6 and 5 pounds for $10), or make up an example of your own, to defend your answer.
followUps: In the grapes example, what is the unit price of each deal, and what does it tell you about the two deals?
Can you build a pair of deals where the bigger amount costs more per unit? How did you choose the numbers?
Besides unit price, what else might a shopper think about before choosing a deal?

t_d4b81364dc58.prompt: A pump moves 28 liters of water in 7 minutes. What is the unit rate in liters per minute?
t_d4b81364dc58.explanation: Divide liters by minutes: 28 ÷ 7 = 4 liters per minute.

t_ee445128d616.prompt: A ticket costs $5. Which sentence expresses the same rate using “for each”?

choices.text: The cost is 1 ticket for each $5.
The cost is $5 for each ticket.
The cost is $5 for each dollar.
The cost is 5 tickets for each dollar.

t_ee445128d616.explanation: “$5 per ticket” means $5 for each 1 ticket.

t_bd27848ec004.prompt: A car travels 243 miles using 9 gallons of gas. What is its rate in miles per gallon?
t_bd27848ec004.explanation: For miles per gallon, divide miles by gallons: 243 ÷ 9 = 27 miles per gallon.

t_a08185eecce7.prompt: A printer makes 11 labels per minute. Write this unit rate using “for each.”
t_a08185eecce7.answer: The printer makes 11 labels for each minute.

t_71ac242981b6.prompt: For a rate of 24 ounces for 3 servings, find ounces per serving by dividing 3 by 24.
t_71ac242981b6.explanation: For ounces per serving, divide ounces by servings: 24 ÷ 3.

t_4465978e6a3f.prompt: A cyclist rides 42 miles in 3 hours. What is the cyclist’s speed?
t_4465978e6a3f.explanation: Divide the distance by the time: 42 ÷ 3 = 14 miles per hour.

t_32cca4e7ee39.prompt: Market A sells 6 pounds of beans for $10.20. Market B sells 8 pounds for $12.80. Which is the better buy?

choices.text: Market A because $10.20 is less than $12.80
Market B because 8 pounds cost less per package

t_32cca4e7ee39.explanation: Market A costs $10.20 ÷ 6 = $1.70 per pound. Market B costs $12.80 ÷ 8 = $1.60 per pound, so Market B has the lower unit price.

t_daa1654fc756.prompt: A delivery van travels 72 miles per hour for 2.5 hours. How far does it travel?

t_b47d162bfb4a.prompt: A store sells 9 pounds of peaches for $13.50. Find the unit price and state what it tells you.
t_b47d162bfb4a.explanation: Divide the cost by the number of pounds: $13.50 ÷ 9 = $1.50 per pound.

t_45383710d817.prompt: A boat travels 252 miles at 63 miles per hour. How many hours does the trip take? Include the unit.
t_45383710d817.explanation: Divide the distance by the speed: 252 ÷ 63 = 4 hours.

t_45e09f7666f0.prompt: A classmate says, “35% is 35 squares, so if I shade 35 squares on a grid with 50 squares, that is still 35%.” Do you agree? Argue with your partner using the 100-grid from today. What is the whole, and why does it matter?
followUps: Where in your notes can you point to the whole on a 100-grid, and how does that help you check a percent?
If a grid had 50 squares and 25 were shaded, would that also be 50%? What would you compare it to?
How is ‘per 100' like ‘per hour’ from the unit rates we started with? What number comes after the word per?

t_30dd64232870.prompt: Two students write 35% as a decimal. One says 3.5 and the other says 0.035. A third says 0.35. Who is right, and how could you convince the other two without just telling them the rule?
followUps: How can a 100-grid with 35 squares shaded show that 35% is 0.35 of the whole grid?
Both 35/100 and 7/20 equal 35%. How does dividing both rows of a ratio table by 5 show that they are the same?
Where would 35% sit on a double number line? Is it closer to 0 or to 50, and does 0.035 or 3.5 fit that spot?

t_30f9cd4fd002.explanation: Percent means per 100, so 28% means 28 for every 100.

t_90826f597e1f.prompt: Which fraction is equal to 32% in simplest form?
t_90826f597e1f.explanation: 32% is 32/100. Dividing the numerator and denominator by 4 gives 8/25.

t_91c7c3183de5.prompt: A double number line has matching marks for 0% and 0 squares, 25% and 25 squares, 50% and 50 squares, 75% and 75 squares, and 100% and 100 squares. Where does 65% belong?
t_91c7c3183de5.explanation: On this double number line, each percent matches the same number of squares out of 100.

t_b6f35601922b.prompt: A 100-grid has 42 shaded squares. Write the shaded amount as a percent and as a fraction in simplest form.
t_b6f35601922b.explanation: 42 shaded squares out of 100 represent 42%. The fraction 42/100 simplifies to 21/50.

t_4c71dbc4bd9c.prompt: On a double number line from 0% to 100%, 20% belongs above 80 squares.
t_4c71dbc4bd9c.explanation: 20% matches 20 squares out of 100, not 80 squares.

t_0bfe189d9c79.prompt: A classmate says: “To find the whole when you know the part and its percent, just find the percent of the part. 40% of 12 is 4.8, so that is the answer.” Does that make sense? Decide with a partner whether you agree, and use a ratio table or a check to back up your view.
followUps: Is 12 the whole or the part in the club problem? How does the place where 12 sits in the table show that?
Would you expect the class to have more than 12 students or fewer? How does that help you spot an answer that cannot be right?
How can you check the answer 30 by going the other way, starting from 100% and finding 40%?

t_f19484c357f2.prompt: Two students find 35% of 80 beads. Student A divides 80 by 20 to get 5% is 4 beads, then multiplies by 7. Student B finds 10% is 8, then 30% is 24, then adds half of 8 to get 28. Which method is better? Take a side, or argue that it depends, and explain your reasoning.
followUps: Do both methods give the same answer? Why must they, even though the steps are different?
Which method would you pick for 15% of 60 minutes, and which for 75% of 24 cups? Why?
What does each row of the ratio table tell you, and which arrows show the multiplying or dividing?

t_36bb9c43c20f.prompt: A box has 64 markers. Twenty-five percent are red. How many markers are red?
t_36bb9c43c20f.explanation: 25% is one quarter. One quarter of 64 is 16.

t_7155fd95a379.prompt: Twelve is 30% of a number. Find the number.
t_7155fd95a379.explanation: If 30% is 12, then 10% is 4 and 100% is 40.

t_1fd7a77eb437.explanation: 10% of 80 is 8 and 5% is 4. Together, 15% is 12.

t_fc7b77511206.prompt: If 24 is 40% of a number, the whole number is 60.

t_4c46ef1fcb7c.prompt: A club has 18 members, which is 45% of all the students who signed up. How many students signed up?
t_4c46ef1fcb7c.explanation: If 45% is 18, then 5% is 2. So 100%, or 20 groups of 5%, is 40.

t_c2b0faf27200.prompt: Imagine a classmate says, ‘In a ratio problem, a table is always better than a tape diagram.’ Do you agree? Think about problems where you split a total into parts and problems where you scale a ratio up or down. Be ready to defend your choice with a reason.
followUps: Which kind of problem makes a tape diagram feel faster to you, and why?
Can you think of a problem where either tool works equally well? How would the two answers compare?
What would you say to a classmate who picks a tool only because it is the one they like best?

t_90da8fcc69f9.prompt: Suppose a student writes, ‘Finding a percent of a number is just multiplying by the percent.’ Is that a complete explanation of what is happening? Talk about what a percent is a rate of, and what the whole is. What would make an explanation convincing to someone who was not there?
followUps: What should a good written explanation always name before it describes any steps?
How can you check that an answer to a percent problem makes sense, for example whether it should be smaller or larger than the whole?
If two students use different methods and get the same answer, are both explanations equally strong? Why or why not?

t_defb882aba1c.prompt: A ratio of red tiles to blue tiles is 18 to 30. What is the ratio in simplest form?
t_defb882aba1c.explanation: Divide both parts of 18 to 30 by 6. The simplified ratio is 3 to 5.

t_e312e6d0d72e.prompt: A mural uses 3 blue tiles for every 5 white tiles. In a ratio table, the blue-tile row is 3, 9, 15 and the white-tile row is 5, 15, __. What number belongs in the blank?
t_e312e6d0d72e.explanation: The blue-tile count goes from 3 to 15 by multiplying by 5. Multiply the white-tile count, 5, by 5 as well: 25.

t_5eec2d006752.prompt: A jar has red and green beads in the ratio 2 to 7, with 54 beads altogether. A tape diagram has 2 equal boxes for red beads and 7 equal boxes for green beads. How many beads does each box represent?
t_5eec2d006752.explanation: The diagram has 2 + 7 = 9 equal boxes. Divide 54 beads by 9 boxes to find 6 beads per box.

t_1c2a3e244272.prompt: A runner records 4 miles in 32 minutes and 8 miles in 64 minutes. Explain in words how a ratio table can show the time for 10 miles. Include the calculation and why the answer makes sense.
t_1c2a3e244272.answer: The time for 4 miles is 32 minutes, so the unit rate is 32 ÷ 4 = 8 minutes per mile. For 10 miles, 10 × 8 = 80 minutes. This makes sense because 10 miles is 2.5 times 4 miles, and 80 minutes is 2.5 times 32 minutes.
t_1c2a3e244272.explanation: A complete response identifies the matching distance and time, scales both quantities by the same factor (or uses the unit rate), and checks that the result is consistent.

f_ad7d82259716.question: Why is 3:2 not the same as 2:3?
f_ad7d82259716.answer: The order of the numbers follows the order of the words. With 3 apples and 2 bananas, apples to bananas is 3:2. Bananas to apples is 2:3. They compare the same fruit, but they answer different questions. The first word names the first number.

f_0642016106b2.question: How do I find the whole in a part-to-whole ratio?
f_0642016106b2.answer: Add the parts together. With 3 apples and 2 bananas, the whole is 3 + 2 = 5 pieces of fruit. So apples to all fruit is 3:5, not 3:2. Writing 3:2 for apples to all fruit is a common mistake, because it leaves out the apples already counted in the whole.

f_e09076b49402.question: Can I write a ratio as a fraction, like 3/2?
f_e09076b49402.answer: Not in this lesson. Write a ratio as words, as a:b or as a to b. A ratio such as 3:2 compares two quantities. It is not a fraction. Use 3:2, 3 to 2, or 3 apples for every 2 bananas.

f_e8a58f177e89.question: Can I just add the same number to both quantities to make an equivalent ratio?
f_e8a58f177e89.answer: No. Adding 3 to both numbers of 3:2 gives 6:5, which is not equivalent to 3:2. To keep the same comparison, multiply both quantities by the same number. Multiplying 3:2 by 2 gives 6:4.

f_f0292912f103.question: How do I find a missing value in a ratio table?
f_f0292912f103.answer: Look at the column where you know both numbers and the column where you know one. Work out the number that takes the known quantity to its new value. For 3:2 and 15 apples, 3 × 5 = 15, so the multiplier is 5. Then multiply the other quantity by the same number: 2 × 5 = 10 bananas.

f_4a080664b2de.question: How do I know if two ratios are equivalent?
f_4a080664b2de.answer: Find the multiplier that takes the first number of the first ratio to the first number of the second. Then check that the same multiplier works on the second numbers. For 3:2 and 12:8, both 3 × 4 = 12 and 2 × 4 = 8, so they are equivalent. If the multiplier works for one number but not the other, the ratios are not equivalent.

f_900333ab33c1.question: Why do all the boxes have to be the same size?
f_900333ab33c1.answer: Each box is one unit, and every unit is worth the same amount. If the boxes are different sizes, you cannot say that one box is 4 or 5. Check that the boxes in both rows match before you label anything.

f_1efa97562de5.question: The problem gives me 20 fruit in all. Why do I divide by 5 and not by 3?
f_1efa97562de5.answer: Match the number you are given to the boxes it covers. The 20 is the whole, so it covers all the boxes: 3 + 2 = 5 boxes. Then 20 ÷ 5 = 4 for one unit. Only a given part, such as 15 apples, covers just its own boxes, so you would divide 15 by 3.

f_d74bfaccb9d3.question: What do I do when the problem gives a difference, like 8 more puppies than kittens?
f_d74bfaccb9d3.answer: Look at the diagram and ask what the extra boxes stand for. Puppies to kittens is 5:3, so puppies have 5 − 3 = 2 extra boxes. Those 2 boxes are worth 8, so one unit is 8 ÷ 2 = 4. Then multiply to find each quantity.

f_9222ed6aa4cf.question: Why do I divide 12 by 3 and not 3 by 12?
f_9222ed6aa4cf.answer: Look at the word after ‘per’. In 12 miles in 3 hours, we want miles per hour, so hours is the quantity after ‘per’. That is the number you divide by: 12 ÷ 3 = 4 miles per hour. Check by multiplying back: 4 × 3 = 12.

f_7f20f72f4359.question: Do I have to write the units, or is just 4 enough?
f_7f20f72f4359.answer: Write the units. A rate compares two different units, so 4 alone does not say what is being counted. Write 4 miles per hour. The units tell what the 4 is about and which quantity was divided by.

f_b03781f973dd.question: Is ‘per’ different from ‘for each’?
f_b03781f973dd.answer: No. They mean the same thing. ‘Per’ means ‘for each 1.’ So $2 per notebook and $2 for each notebook say the same unit rate. In a ratio table, both describe the column where the second quantity is 1.

f_bb7ba7c7b86c.question: Why can’t I just compare the total prices to find the better buy?
f_bb7ba7c7b86c.answer: Total prices only work when you get the same amount. Store A charges $6 for 4 pounds of rice and Store B charges $14 for 10 pounds. $6 is less than $14, but Store B gives you much more rice. Find the unit price of each deal. Store A is $1.50 per pound and Store B is $1.40 per pound, so Store B is the better buy.

f_dfb4cb615b56.question: When do I multiply and when do I divide in a speed problem?
f_dfb4cb615b56.answer: Multiply to find a distance: distance = speed × time. A car at 55 miles per hour for 4 hours goes 55 × 4 = 220 miles. Divide to find a time: time = distance ÷ speed. A hiker at 3 miles per hour needs 9 ÷ 3 = 3 hours to walk 9 miles. A ratio table with 1 hour in one column helps you see which operation to use. Check by multiplying back.

f_d8de4ddf3269.question: What if both deals have the same unit price?
f_d8de4ddf3269.answer: Then neither deal is better. Three pounds of grapes for $6 and 5 pounds for $10 both cost $2 per pound, so they are the same deal. A bigger pack is not always cheaper per unit. Always write each unit price with its unit, such as dollars per pound.

f_ecc9d89d1227.question: Why is the whole always 100 squares, even when only a few squares are shaded?
f_ecc9d89d1227.answer: A percent compares a part to 100. On a 100-grid the whole grid is 100 squares, and the shaded squares are the percent. If 8 squares are shaded, that is 8 per 100, or 8%. The shaded squares are the part, not the whole.

f_d3e28ac25d9a.question: How do I write 35% as a fraction and a decimal?
f_d3e28ac25d9a.answer: 35% means 35 per 100, so the fraction is 35/100. Divide the top and bottom by 5 to get 7/20. The decimal is 0.35. Check it on the grid: 35 squares out of 100 is 0.35 of the grid. It is not 3.5 or 0.035.

f_ae5c7015d235.question: How do I place a percent on a double number line?
f_ae5c7015d235.answer: Put 0% above 0 and 100% above 100 squares. Space the ticks evenly, because uneven spaces give wrong positions. 50% sits halfway, above 50. To mark 40%, find 40 on the bottom line, then put 40% directly above it. You can shade 40 squares on a grid to check.

f_057a6548a116.question: In 35% of 80 beads, why is the answer not 35 beads?
f_057a6548a116.answer: The 35 comes from 35% of 100, where the whole is 100. Here the whole is 80 beads, so 100% goes above 80. Then 5% is 80 ÷ 20 = 4 beads, and 35% is 7 × 4 = 28 beads.

f_ea4152e4a84b.question: When I am given a part and its percent, how do I find the whole?
f_ea4152e4a84b.answer: Put the part under its percent in the ratio table, then scale up to 100%. If 12 students are 40% of the class, then 10% is 3 students and 100% is 30 students. Do not find 40% of 12. The number 12 is the part, not the whole.

f_2bd256487390.question: How can I check my answer?
f_2bd256487390.answer: Go the other way. If 12 is 40% of 30, then finding 40% of 30 should give back 12. For a part, check that your answer is smaller than the whole when the percent is under 100%. For example, 28 beads is less than 80 beads.

f_035f0c0bf421.question: Can I use a calculator or my notes?
f_035f0c0bf421.answer: No. Clear your desk except for a pencil, an eraser and a ruler. Use tables, tape diagrams and unit rates to work out each answer by hand.

f_8e8516ba9235.question: What should I do if I can’t remember how to start a problem?
f_8e8516ba9235.answer: Pick a tool you know. A ratio table or a tape diagram works for many problems. Find the whole and the parts, or find 1 unit or 10% first, then scale up. Show every step, because your work shows your thinking.

f_38a18ca35722.question: What makes a good written explanation?
f_38a18ca35722.answer: Name the whole, say what you did to each row of the table or each part of the diagram, and check that the answer makes sense. Your reasoning matters more than how long your answer is.

f_8a376650c839.question: When will I get my test results?
f_8a376650c839.answer: Results will be shared once the papers are marked. Next time the class will go over the test and talk about the unit.
